meta.method: Each row is a real conceptual correspondence found by reading both frameworks' descriptive text and this book's chapters, not a code-similarity guess. Not every AP topic or CA standard appears here -- pairs with no honest counterpart are left out of this file and covered instead in alignment/standards_alignment.md's gaps view. A topic can appear in more than one row when it genuinely corresponds to more than one thing on the other side.

strength_definitions.strong: same skill, same depth, taught by the same book chapters
strength_definitions.partial: same skill but different depth, scope, or emphasis -- one framework asks for more or less than the other
strength_definitions.related: adjacent territory, but close reading shows the two are not actually testing the same thing

crosswalk.note: Both are the team-roles/collaborative-tools practice, not book content -- pair programming and shared tools either way. Carried the same way on both sides: continuously, through lab pair work and the Create Performance Task.

CA files 'use collaboration tools to connect with people of different cultures and careers' under Impacts of Computing, not alongside its own AP.21 -- a different emphasis (breadth of who you connect with) than AP CSP's CRD-1.A (diverse perspectives improve the artifact you're building).

AP CSP's CRD-2.C/D only asks students to describe events and inputs/outputs conceptually; CA's AP.15 requires actually building an event-driven artifact (a button, a timer). This book's chap01/chap05 material satisfies the AP side but not the CA side -- CA asks for more here, not less.
Both are the in-code documentation habit -- chap04's docstrings and development-plan material satisfy this directly on both sides.

AP CSP's CRD-2.F (design phase) is satisfied by chap04's development plan alone. CA's AP.18 specifically requires incorporating feedback from a broad audience of users -- chap04's process is solo and technical, never audience-facing. CA asks for more here too.

Both are the same gap, not just a similar one: AP's CRD-2.H (acknowledging code taken from another source) and CA's AP.19 (license limitations on using libraries) are the same underlying idea -- crediting and respecting others' code -- and neither has any counterpart anywhere in the book, even though chap04/chap08 use borrowed libraries. A single supplement would close both at once.

Both are iterative testing and debugging aimed at correctness. chap04 and chap07 (doctest) carry this on both sides. CA's usability/accessibility clauses go slightly further than AP CSP's error-focused framing, but the core overlap is solid.

Tempting to pair these -- both are nominally 'troubleshooting' -- but CA CS.3's own worked examples are network connectivity and help-desk guidelines, a systems-level skill, not code debugging. Every chapter's Debugging section carries AP CRD-1.4; it does not carry CA CS.3. Logged as 'related' specifically so this book doesn't get credited for a standard it doesn't actually teach.

Same content: representing real-world data (characters, numbers, color) in bits. Neither is carried by this book. Both real gaps as of 2026-08-09 -- previously routed to CS50T Multimedia, dropped per teacher confirmation it hasn't been taught since year one. The Pico I2C chapter is a partial, non-closing touchpoint for hex/byte notation; see apcsp.json's 2.1 note.

CA DA.9's own worked example is file-size-vs-quality tradeoffs across image formats, which is data compression -- the same territory as AP's 2.2. But DA.9's stated scope is broader (storage location, cost, reliability, privacy), not compression alone. Both real gaps as of 2026-08-09, same reason as the 2.1/DA.8 pair above -- no replacement identified for either.
Both are 'group related values so the program can treat them as one thing instead of separate variables.' chap09 (Lists), chap10 (Dictionaries), and chap11 (Tuples) satisfy both.

AP CSP's 3.6/3.7 only ask students to write and evaluate conditionals. CA's AP.14 asks students to justify a choice between control structures (e.g., multiple ifs vs. a nested if) on readability/performance grounds -- a step beyond writing them. chap05 provides the raw material; the comparative-justification framing isn't explicit in the book.

CA AP.14's own worked example is literally 'multiple if statements versus a nested if statement' -- a closer textual match than the 3.6 pairing above. Same gap: chap05 teaches nested conditionals but not the comparative readability/performance justification CA asks for.

CA AP.14's own worked example is comparing recursive vs. iterative Fibonacci -- and chap06 has a section literally named 'Fibonacci,' built on chap05's recursion. But per the AP index's 3.8 note, this book has no `while` loop anywhere, so the 'iterative' side of that comparison is thinner here than the recursive side. Both frameworks want the comparison; the book demonstrates only half of it well.

Both are 'build an algorithm through incremental refinement.' chap07's step-by-step construction of `uses_any`/linear search is a direct match for CA AP.12's 'design algorithms... using a combination of original and existing algorithms.'
Same pairing as 3.2 above, from the more concrete (lists specifically) side.

chap09's 'Sorting lists' section uses Python's built-in sort, which is the 'existing algorithm' half of CA AP.12's search-and-sort framing. It doesn't have students design a sort themselves, so this is thinner than the 3.9/AP.12 pairing above.

Worth flagging precisely because it's easy to overstate: AP CSP names binary search as its own required topic (3.11), but CA AP.12's language is generic ('searching and sorting algorithms'), satisfied by linear search alone. CA does not specifically require binary search the way AP CSP does -- so the book's binary-search gap (see the AP index's 3.11 note) is a sharper problem for AP than it is for CA.
Both are procedural decomposition. chap03/chap04 carry this directly.
Same pairing, from the 'write your own well-designed procedure' side.
Both are 'use a library instead of writing it yourself.' chap02 (`import`), chap04 (jupyturtle), chap08 (`re`) carry both directly.

CA AP.12's own worked example specifically mentions randomization algorithms for games (dice rolls, card selection). AP CSP treats random values as their own topic (3.15) rather than folding them into 'algorithms.' Same chap12 evidence carries both, but the two frameworks frame it differently enough that this is 'related' rather than 'strong.'

Both touch 'models of real processes,' but from different angles: AP's 3.16 is about trading off realism for repeatability/cost; CA's DA.11 is about refining a model against real-world observations. Neither is carried by this book, and they'd need different supplements even though they sound adjacent -- flagged so the two gaps aren't accidentally treated as one problem.

CA AP.14 explicitly folds an informal efficiency/performance discussion into its control-structure comparison ('theoretical understanding of execution time... a quantitative analysis is not expected' -- the same no-Big-O boundary AP CSP draws). But AP's 3.17 is a dedicated topic covering more ground (heuristics, decision vs. optimization problems) than CA's control-structure-scoped mention.
Both Little Brother's territory; not itemized further at the sub-topic level since neither framework routes this content through this book.
Same as above.
Adjacent (network reliability vs. network security) rather than the same idea, but both are Little Brother's territory either way.
Both are encryption/decryption and the symmetric-vs-asymmetric distinction, both explicitly excluding the underlying math. Little Brother's territory on both sides.
Both are 'computing's effects can be positive, negative, or both, and not always what the designer intended.' Little Brother's territory.
Both are algorithmic/design bias and the need to actively test for it. Little Brother's territory.
Both are intellectual property law's beneficial and harmful effects on innovation. Little Brother's territory.
AP's IOC-2.A is broad privacy risk from data collection; CA's IC.29 is specifically automated/non-evident collection. Overlapping but CA is narrower. Little Brother's territory either way.
Both are evaluating privacy policy/law tradeoffs for safety, law, and ethics. Little Brother's territory.
